title: Movement and speed
subtitle: swerve, drift, crawl, tear along; speed, rate, pace
summary: Learn the verbs English uses for particular kinds of movement, the verbs for moving fast and slowly, and the four nouns speed, rate, pace and velocity.

lesson.heading: What moves where
rows: sail on rivers, across the sea
flow / run through towns and villages
lesson.note: Move is the basic verb for all movement, but remember it also means to move to a new house or flat: We've moved. Do you want our new address?

lesson.heading: Particular types of movement
lesson.text: Things often have their own verb of movement. Learn each one as a collocation, with a phrase or sentence to fix it.

examples.text: The car **swerved** to avoid a dog which had run into the road.
examples.note: swerve = move suddenly to the side
flutter = move gently from side to side

examples.text: The leaves **stirred** in the light breeze.
The trees **swayed** back and forth as the wind grew stronger.
examples.note: sway = move slowly from side to side

lesson.heading: Fast and slow movement
rows: The traffic was crawling along because of the roadworks.
The train was just creeping along at about 20 miles per hour.
move more slowly than is necessary
The donkey was plodding along the road.
A car came round the bend and tore along the road at high speed.
Seconds later, a police car shot past after it.
do something quickly because time is short
Everyone was hurrying to get their shopping done before closing time.
The plane was cruising at a height of 30,000 metres.

lesson.heading: These verbs used more widely
lesson.text: Many of these verbs stretch beyond their first context. A baby **crawls**, an insect **crawls**, a bird's wings **flutter**, a boat **drifts** - and a person can **drift** through life without any sense of direction.

examples.text: The baby **crawled** across the floor before she could walk.
A fish can **shoot** through the water; a plane can **shoot** overhead.
A butterfly's wings **flutter**, and so does washing on the line in the wind.
My thoughts **drifted** to what she had said, and then I **drifted off** to sleep.
She **swayed** slightly as the ship rolled.

lesson.heading: Nouns for speed
rows: We were travelling at high speed.
statistical contexts: rate of increase / decrease
The birth rate is going down.
how you experience something as fast or slow
The lesson was going at a very slow pace.
the velocity of a moving object

lesson.heading: The preposition is at
lesson.text: We say **at** a speed, **at** a rate and **at** a pace - never *in* or *with*. This is one of the most frequent mistakes at this level.

examples.text: The train was travelling **at a speed** of 120 kph.
We were making progress but only **at a very slow pace**.
Trains can travel **at a much faster speed** than buses.

lesson.text: Creep and stir are irregular: creep, crept, crept; and stir doubles the r - stir, stirred, stirred.

exercises.prompt: Pair up the sentences so they make sense.

pairs.left: That tree was swaying back and forth in the wind.
pairs.right: It was moving so much I thought it would break.

pairs.left: The cruise liner is leaving tomorrow.
A cat ran out in front of my car.
pairs.right: I had to swerve hard and nearly ended up in the river.

pairs.left: The most famous river in France is the Seine.
pairs.right: It flows through the capital city.

pairs.left: A train came off the rails yesterday.
pairs.right: It was travelling at 160 kph at the time.

exercises.prompt: The ___ of decline in this species is alarming.
exercises.explanation: Rate is used in statistical contexts: the rate of increase or decrease.

exercises.prompt: I just couldn't stand the ___ of life in the city, so I moved to a small village.
exercises.explanation: Pace shows how you experience something as happening fast or slow.

exercises.prompt: The teacher asked the students to calculate the ___ of a series of objects dropped from a specific height.
exercises.explanation: Velocity is used in technical and scientific contexts.

exercises.prompt: *A: What ___ were you doing at the time?* *B: Oh, about 60 kph, I'd say.*
exercises.explanation: Speed is the general word, used for vehicles, developments and changes.

exercises.prompt: Match each verb of movement with what it describes.

pairs.right: move gently from side to side, as a flag does
move slowly from side to side, as trees do

exercises.prompt: Does the verb describe fast movement or slow movement?

options: We were making progress but only at a very slow pace.
We were making progress but only in a very slow pace.
We were making progress but only with a very slow pace.
We were making progress but only on a very slow pace.
exercises.explanation: We say at a speed, at a rate and at a pace.

exercises.statement: 'Pierre creeped down the stairs making as little noise as possible' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: The past tense of creep is crept: Pierre crept down the stairs.

exercises.statement: 'The baby stired but didn't wake up' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: The past tense of stir doubles the r: The baby stirred but didn't wake up.

exercises.statement: 'The old man swayed a little but didn't fall over' is correct English.
exercises.explanation: Correct - sway means to move slowly from side to side; swerve would mean he moved suddenly sideways.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to describe a car on a bend.
exercises.answer: A car came round the bend and tore along the road at high speed.
exercises.explanation: Tear along means to move at high speed; note at high speed.

exercises.prompt: The traffic was ___ along because of the roadworks.
exercises.explanation: Crawl and creep both describe moving very slowly.
